transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-07
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Elena Torres (Northbridge Security Lead), David Ng (Northbridge CTO), Sana Patel (Northbridge IT Ops)

Summary (auto):
High-level review of what Redwood captures in admin/audit logs, discussion of offsite export (S3 + SIEM streaming), retention and cold archival options, KMS handling for exported logs, RBAC/SSO mapping for audit attribution, and SOC2 evidence. Customer wanted to confirm exact fields captured, encryption and key ownership model, and options for long-term immutable storage.

Topics:
- Admin activity events schema (who/what/where/when/why)
- Export integrations (S3, streaming, SIEM connectors)
- Retention baseline and archival/immutable options
- KMS and key separation for exports
- Attribution and RBAC/SSO mapping
- Evidence for SOC 2 audits

[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. We're gonna run through what Redwood captures for admin activity and the export/retention story. Priya and Marcus are on to cover more technical bits.
[00:22] Elena Torres: Thanks Jordan, quick context: Northbridge does consulting for financials, we're bound by internal retention rules plus some client residency constraints. We need to be sure logs are immutable and that we can ship them to our Splunk instance.
[00:35] Priya Desai: Perfect, we hear that a lot. Quick agenda: types of admin events we capture, what fields you get, how export works (S3 + streaming), KMS behavior, and options for long term cold storage.
[00:50] David Ng: Also curious how user attribution works when folks are SSOing through Okta, and what happens with service tokens and API keys.
[01:05] Marcus Lee: Yeah, attribution is a big one. We'll show the event schema which has actor.identity, actor.method (okta/saml/api-key/service), resource.target, action.type, timestamp, request_id and sometimes context like IP and region. There can be occasional mis-tags in the auto transcript, like we sometimes see K-V cash instead of KV cache in reports, sorry for the bad auto-captures.
[01:40] Elena Torres: Ok, show me an example event.
[01:45] Priya Desai: Example: {"timestamp": "2025-09-30T18:12:05Z", "actor": {"id": "u-2345", "type": "user", "auth_method": "saml"}, "action": "model.deploy", "resource": {"model_id": "red-7b-quant"}, "result": "success", "meta": {"ip": "203.0.113.45", "region": "us-west-2"}}
[02:20] Sana Patel: That sample is good, but we need to ensure the identity ties back to our internal directory - like Okta user IDs. How hard is mapping?
[02:31] Priya Desai: We support passing through the identity claims that come from SAML/SCIM provisioning. In hosted mode we store the login mapping and the raw assertion; in Private deployments you can configure the assertion passthrough so events have your internal user IDs. There's also an option to include an external_user_id field for SIEM correlation.
[02:55] David Ng: And for service accounts, do you log the API key creation/deletion and token rotations?
[03:05] Marcus Lee: Yes, creation, delete, rotate, revoke are all recorded as admin.events. We log old_id/new_id on rotation and include references to the policy that allowed it.
[03:22] Elena Torres: What about the fidelity — do you capture prompt contents or model outputs in the admin log?
[03:30] Priya Desai: Short answer: Not by default. Admin logs capture metadata about requests and which model was called, but not user prompt text. For compliance you can enable separate data audit streams for request/response bodies with access controls — that's a separate export and needs additional encryption and retention controls.
[03:58] Elena Torres: Good, that helps. Next question: export options — we want to push to S3 (immutable), but also to our on-prem Splunk.
[04:10] Marcus Lee: We support several export patterns: periodic S3 batches (parquet/json) with lifecycle rules, streaming via Kafka or an HTTPS webhook for SIEMs, and direct connector to Splunk HTTP event collector. For S3 we can put objects with server-side encryption and we can optionally sign them with a customer-managed KMS key.
[04:40] David Ng: If we use our KMS key, do you have access to it?
[04:45] Priya Desai: No, if you supply a CMK (customer-managed key) on supported clouds, Redwood does not have plaintext access to the exported objects. We use envelope encryption; Redwood can only write ciphertext blobs. Key rotation is honored — if a re-wrap is required we provide a clear process but we never hold your master key.
[05:10] Elena Torres: Is there support for WORM (write once read many) or object lock on S3?
[05:18] Marcus Lee: Yes, we can configure S3 Object Lock with retention mode for compliance (governance or compliance mode) as part of the export bucket config. For hosted customers we can coordinate setting the bucket and the lock policy; for Private you manage your own bucket.
[05:40] Sana Patel: For legal holds, how would we temporarily retain beyond retention?
[05:45] Priya Desai: The recommended approach is object locking plus a separate long-term archive bucket with different lifecycle policies. You can also request an export snapshot if you need to create an immutable evidence package for an audit.
[06:05] Elena Torres: About retention defaults — what's Redwood's baseline?
[06:10] Jordan Kim: Hosted defaults are 90 days for admin events. You can configure longer for Dedicated/Private. For compliance customers we often do 365 days or custom S3 archival to cold storage.
[06:25] David Ng: If we want seven years retention for some clients, how does that impact cost/ingest?
[06:31] Marcus Lee: Long retention is offloaded to your own archival storage (S3 Glacier/Archive) — Redwood will export and you pay Redwood export fees plus your cloud storage. We can estimate the storage cost in the POC.
[06:50] Elena Torres: We need immutable chain of custody — do you provide signing or hash chaining of exported batches?
[06:58] Priya Desai: We can include SHA-256 manifests for each export and optionally sign manifests with a Redwood signing key. If you need end-to-end verifiable chain of custody we recommend you keep the exported objects in a bucket with Object Lock and enable server-side encryption with your CMK, and also maintain a separate manifest in your control plane.
[07:30] Sana Patel: Can we push logs in near real-time?
[07:34] Marcus Lee: Yes, streaming mode is near real-time. Typical latency is under 10s for events through our streaming pipeline to Kafka or webhook endpoints, assuming network conditions are normal. There may be bursts that introduce a few seconds more.
[07:50] Elena Torres: Are there throttles or backpressure considerations if our Splunk endpoint is slow?
[07:55] Priya Desai: We support configurable retry/backoff and dead-lettering. For slow consumers we recommend S3 as a buffer, or Kafka with durable retention so you can replay.
[08:12] David Ng: Regarding the schema — do you support custom fields or enrichment on export?
[08:18] Marcus Lee: Exports include a metadata.enrichments array. You can ask Redwood to enrich with customer_id, tenancy_id, or tagging fields. We also support a transform hook in Private deployments for custom enrichment prior to export.
[08:40] Elena Torres: For the SOC 2 evidence, what artifacts do you provide?
[08:45] Jordan Kim: We provide SOC 2 report redacted for public use, plus a bundle for SOC2 auditors that includes architecture diagrams, control descriptions, sample audit logs, encryption details, and KMS usage patterns. We can redact customer-specific data on request.
[09:05] Elena Torres: Do you provide live access to audit logs for auditors?
[09:10] Priya Desai: We typically provide a snapshot export and a dedicated read-only access period through our console. For enterprise audits we do temporary S3 access to a pre-configured export layered with the appropriate permission.
[09:30] David Ng: If you give auditors temporary access, how do you prevent data exfil?
[09:35] Marcus Lee: We use short-lived pre-signed URLs or limited STS tokens and restrict access to specific prefixes. Access is logged and reversible, and we can enforce IP allowlists for auditor access.
[09:58] Elena Torres: What about redaction — can we automatically redact PII from exports?
[10:05] Priya Desai: We offer a redaction pipeline that can remove or truncate certain fields before export. For high sensitivity we recommend doing redaction as part of the transform hook in your Private deployment or via our export lambda that runs in your account.
[10:30] Sana Patel: Does Redwood capture failed login attempts and MFA related events?
[10:35] Marcus Lee: Yes, authentication flow events (login.success, login.failure, mfa.challenge, mfa.success/failure) are captured with context such as reason codes.
[10:52] Elena Torres: Is admin console activity like role changes, RBAC grants, and policy updates included?
[10:58] Priya Desai: All admin plane changes — RBAC edits, role grants, policy changes, route updates, and credential operations — are audited. We capture pre/post state for critical operations when possible.
[11:20] David Ng: How are role names mapped for external identity providers?
[11:25] Marcus Lee: We map incoming SAML role attributes to internal roles; you can provide a role mapping configuration. For Private deployments that mapping lives in your control plane.
[11:40] Elena Torres: Any known gaps?
[11:44] Priya Desai: A few customers have asked for deeper lineage for model artifacts (e.g., training data tags). We currently focus on serving/inference audit; training lineage is not first class in the audit stream. Also very large embedding stores can create heavy audit volume for some workloads; we usually sample or aggregate those events.
[12:10] Sana Patel: Can you keep logs in-region for data residency?
[12:15] Jordan Kim: Yes, region pinning is supported. Exports can be to a bucket in the same region and we can ensure the control plane does not cross region boundaries for Private deployments. Hosted mode supports region selection too, and we have EU/UK/AU regions available.
[12:35] David Ng: For our UK clients we need logs stored in the UK and not leave region. Is that doable in hosted?
[12:41] Marcus Lee: Yes, choose the UK region at onboarding; the audit events and export will remain in-region. For strict jurisdictional controls we advise Private with VPC egress to your storage.
[12:58] Elena Torres: On encryption at rest for internal storage, what's your approach?
[13:03] Priya Desai: Data at rest is encrypted using service-managed keys by default; for more control you can supply a CMK. Logs exported to your S3 can be encrypted with your key. In transit we use TLS 1.2/1.3.
[13:30] Sana Patel: Are audit logs tamper-evident within Redwood's console?
[13:35] Marcus Lee: We index logs immutably within our storage layer and maintain write-once indexing for events. For extra assurance we provide exported manifests and signing as discussed.
[13:50] David Ng: How do you handle cross-tenant events for multi-tenant infra?
[13:55] Priya Desai: Events are scoped with tenancy_id and strict separation at the storage layer — you cannot query other tenants' events. We can provide an auditor role that has read-only access to a specific tenant prefix for audit purposes.
[14:20] Elena Torres: What about retention of exported logs if a customer leaves — do you keep a copy?
[14:26] Jordan Kim: No, we do not hold retained copies beyond contractual obligations. When a contract ends we remove tenant data per the contract; customer-owned exports remain in your storage. We provide a complete export package during offboarding.
[14:50] Sana Patel: For the POC, we want to validate streaming to Splunk and verify that Okta IDs show up. What's the best approach?
[14:58] Priya Desai: We propose a 2-week POC: 1) set up a mirror Splunk HEC endpoint or temp bucket, 2) enable streaming for admin events, 3) run scripted actions (user login, key rotation, role change) and verify correlation. We will provide scripts and sample queries.
[15:25] Marcus Lee: We'll also include a test that simulates a burst to exercise backpressure handling.
[15:32] Elena Torres: Sounds good. Slight question: how are deleted logs handled — can they be recovered?
[15:38] Marcus Lee: Deleted logs in Redwood's managed store are subject to retention and purge policies; for recovery we recommend relying on your exported copies as the source of truth. We can retain backups for a short recovery window if contractually agreed.
[15:55] David Ng: On legal/procurement front, any standard clauses we should expect around audit log exports and encryption?
[16:02] Jordan Kim: Standard SOW covers data handling, encryption standards, and export responsibilities. We can share a sample DPA and S3 export appendix.
[16:20] Elena Torres: About the export format, do you have a stable schema versioning so our parsers don't break?
[16:26] Priya Desai: Yes, we version the event schema. We maintain backward compatibility and publish a changelog. For breaking changes we provide a migration window and tooling to map old->new fields.
[16:44] Sana Patel: If we want to anonymize certain fields for client demo or training, is that supported?
[16:50] Marcus Lee: We support anonymization patterns and tokenization for PII fields in the export pipeline. You can configure rules or use an external transform to do more advanced PII scrubbing.
[17:08] Elena Torres: For the POC timing — we need it before our Q4 compliance review (mid-November).
[17:14] Jordan Kim: We can do the POC next week; Priya and Marcus will own the technical side and I'll coordinate procurement docs.
[17:27] David Ng: Any limitations on export volume in streaming?
[17:32] Priya Desai: There are throughput limits per tenant on the hosted plane, but for Dedicated and Private we can provision higher throughput. We'll outline expected quotas in the POC plan.
[17:50] Elena Torres: One more: can exported logs be replayed into our analytics pipeline with preserved ordering?
[17:56] Marcus Lee: We include sequence numbers and a partitioning key so replay with ordering is supported, though ordering across partitions is not guaranteed.
[18:12] Sana Patel: What about cost transparency for audit ingestion — can we get per-log-unit breakdown?
[18:18] Jordan Kim: Yes, Console exposes token/event-level breakdowns and export bytes; we can give an estimate for the POC.
[18:35] Elena Torres: Let's talk about the sensitive client data in prompts again — you said not default captured, but how to ensure that?
[18:42] Priya Desai: Keep default logs disabled for request/response bodies; if you enable them, put them into your own encrypted bucket and enforce RBAC. We also have evals and QA tooling that can flag PII — but it's opt-in.
[19:05] David Ng: For our security team, how do we demonstrate controls during a SOC 2 interview?
[19:12] Marcus Lee: We provide control narratives, sample logs, and a walkthrough. We can coordinate a live session with our compliance lead if your auditors want direct Q&A.
[19:30] Elena Torres: Can you summarize the recommended architecture for us?
[19:34] Priya Desai: Sure: Hosted with UK-region pinning, enable streaming to your Splunk HEC for near-real-time, batch exports to a UK S3 with Object Lock + CMK for long term retention, add a transform function to redact any PII, and configure role mapping from Okta to preserve attribution. We'll provide manifests and signed hashes for each export.
[20:05] Jordan Kim: Quick recap of next steps — we'll send SOC2 artifacts, Priya will share POC plan, Marcus will prepare scripts, and we'll target POC kickoff next Tuesday.
[20:18] Elena Torres: That works. Anything else?
[20:22] Sana Patel: Not from Ops.
[20:25] David Ng: No, thank you.
[20:28] Jordan Kim: Thanks all, we'll follow up with an email summarizing action items.
